nodes.label: Theorem
nodes.next_step: Automatic translation needs attention before a proof can be checked.
nodes.statement:
Put $c_1=0$ and $c_{r+1}=F(c_r)$, where
\[
 F(c)=\frac{(1+c)^2}{8(1-c)}.
\]
For all $n\geq1$, all finite $d$, all orthogonal projections
$P_1,\ldots,P_n$ and all density matrices $\rho$,
\[
 -c_n\leq\mu_n\leq1.
\]
The lower bound is attained in dimension $n$ by real codimension-one
projections and a pure state; for $n=1$ the zero projection suffices.
Furthermore $0\leq c_n<1/3$, $c_n\uparrow1/3$, and
\[
 c_2=\frac18,\qquad c_3=\frac{81}{448},\qquad
 c_4=\frac{279841}{1315328},\qquad
 \frac13-c_n\sim\frac{16}{27n}.
\]
Consequently the uniform infimum is $-1/3$, not attained at any finite
length. The upper bound $1$ is attained.

nodes.statement:
For every integer $r\geq6$, $\Th_{3,3,r}$ is connected and twin-free with
metric dimension two. Its repeated eigenvalues are exactly those in the
following table; each listed eigenvalue has multiplicity two, and every
other eigenvalue is simple.
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc|cc}
 r\bmod6&\text{repeated in }L&\text{repeated in }Q&\mm_L&\mm_Q\\\hline
 0&3&1&2&2\\
 1&3&3&2&2\\
 2&\varnothing&\varnothing&1&1\\
 3&1,3&1,3&2&2\\
 4&1,3&\varnothing&2&1\\
 5&\varnothing&\varnothing&1&1
\end{array}
\]
Thus within this subfamily, both equalities hold in residues $0,1,3$;
neither holds in residues $2,5$; and only the Laplacian equality holds
in residue $4$.

nodes.statement:
The graphs $\Th_{3,3,r}$ are connected and twin-free for every $r\geq2$.
Their metric dimension is three for $r=3,5$, and two otherwise.
The spectral table in Corollary~\ref{cor:all-lengths} holds for every
$r\geq3$. For $r=2$, the only repeated Laplacian eigenvalues are
$3-\sqrt2,3+\sqrt2$, both double, and the signless spectrum is simple.
Consequently exactly one equality holds precisely when
\[
 r=2\quad\hbox{or}\quad r\equiv4\pmod6,
\]
and in every such case it is the Laplacian equality.
Both equalities hold precisely for $r\geq6$ with $r\equiv0,1,3\pmod6$.
Neither holds in the other cases. In particular, no graph of this
entire subfamily separates in the signless-equality direction.

nodes.label: Lemma

nodes.statement:
Let $H_1,\ldots,H_r$ be vertex-disjoint finite simple graphs, each with
specified vertices $v_i,w_i$ satisfying $N_{H_i}(w_i)=\{v_i\}$.
Let $F$ be any simple graph on $\{1,\ldots,r\}$.
Obtain $J_F$ from their disjoint union by adding $v_iv_j$ for each
$ij\in E(F)$. Then
\begin{equation}
 \Dom(J_F)=\{S_1\cup\cdots\cup S_r:S_i\in\Dom(H_i)\},\qquad
 D(J_F,x)=\prod_{i=1}^rD(H_i,x).
\end{equation}
If every $H_i$ and $F$ are connected, then $J_F$ is connected.

nodes.label: Proposition
nodes.next_step: Automatic translation needs attention before a proof can be checked.
nodes.statement:
Let $n,r\ge1$ be integers, write $n=\prod_{p\mid n}p^{e_p}$, and set
\[
 D_r(n)=\prod_{p\mid n}p^{\lceil e_p/r\rceil},\qquad
 C_r(n)=\frac{n}{D_r(n)}.
\]
For every integer $s$,
\begin{align}
 \sum_{k=s+1}^{s+n}\left(
 \floor{\frac{k^r}{n}}-\floor{\frac{k^r-1}{n}}\right)&=C_r(n),
 \\
 \prod_{k=s+1}^{s+n}\left(1-2\left(
 \floor{\frac{k^r}{n}}-\floor{\frac{k^r-1}{n}}\right)\right)
 &=(-1)^{C_r(n)}.
\end{align}
For $n>1$, the equality $C_r(n)=n/\rad(n)$ holds exactly when
$r\ge\max_{p\mid n}e_p$; for $n=1$ it holds for every $r\ge1$.
For every $r\ge2$, the product in~\eqref{eq:product-general} equals
$a(n+1)$, independently of $s$.
nodes.title: OEIS A164660, final FORMULA (29 May 2016): Chebyshev numerators and floor products

nodes.statement:
For $p=2$, $s=3$, \eqref{eq:ratio} is
\[
 Q(n)=\frac{\sum_{d\mid n}d^3}{\sum_{e\mid n,\ e\text{ odd}}e^3}
     =\frac{8^{v+1}-1}{7}.
\]
This is A318935, introduced by N. J. A. Sloane on 14 September 2018
as the sum of cubes of the powers of two dividing $n$; Chai Wah Wu gave
its valuation formula that day. Amiram Eldar recorded the equivalent
cubic divisor ratio on 29 October 2026 \cite{cubic}.
The underlying cubic power sum already occurs as $T$ on page~102 of
Lamont's 1982 paper on Cayley integers \cite{lamont}.
It is also a direct weighted consequence:
\[
 Q(n)=1+4\sum_{\substack{d\mid n\\d>1}}m(d)\varphi(d)^3.
\]

nodes.label: Corollary
nodes.next_step: Existing Lean evidence is being checked before new proof work.
nodes.statement:
For $N\geq1$, the number of inputs $n\leq N$ with
$H(n)=4\cdot2^k-3$ is
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{N}{2^k}\right\rfloor-
 \left\lfloor\frac{N}{2^{k+1}}\right\rfloor\quad(k\geq0).
\]
Furthermore,
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{n=1}^N H(n)=N+4\sum_{j\geq1}2^{j-1}
                    \left\lfloor\frac{N}{2^j}\right\rfloor .
\end{equation}
Among the $2^{\ell-1}$ inputs of binary length $\ell\geq1$, the mean
time is $2\ell-1$ and the maximum is $2^{\ell+1}-3$.
The maximum reproduces Wolfram's earlier closed form \cite{wolfram}; the
distribution and mean follow from the individual-input formula above.

and all its other roots of modulus at most one. If a real sequence

nodes.statement:

\]

and A400644, revision 28, COMMENTS, hold for their specified initial
data: $\sqrt{(1+\sqrt5)/2}$ and the square root of the tribonacci
constant, respectively.

nodes.statement:
Let $X$ be MCD, $|X|=2^h$, and write
$C(X)=\{0=c_0<c_1<\cdots<c_h\}$. Then $X$ is homogeneous,
meaning that its isometry group is transitive on points, and
\[
 \operatorname{Is}(X)\cong G_h,\qquad
 G_0=\{1\},\qquad
 G_h=(G_{h-1}\times G_{h-1})\rtimes C_2,
 \qquad |G_h|=2^{2^h-1},
\]
where $C_2$ swaps the two factors. Moreover, for every $p\in X$,
\[
 |\{x:d(p,x)=c_i\}|=2^{i-1}\quad(1\le i\le h).
\]

nodes.label: Corollary
nodes.next_step: Existing Lean evidence is being checked before new proof work.
nodes.statement:
Writing $y=x(t-1)$, one has
\begin{align}
 \sum_{n\geq0}R_n(t)z^n
 &=\frac{t}{(1+z)(\exp(-z/(1+z))-t)},\\
 G(x,t)&=\frac{t-1}{(1-y)(t-\exp(y/(1-y)))}.
\end{align}
Let $s_j=\mathrm{A000262}(j)$, characterized by
$\sum s_j u^j/j!=\exp(u/(1-u))$. Then the modified Riordan recurrence
stated in A131758 is
\begin{equation}
 P_n(t)=n!(t-1)^n+\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\binom nj s_{n-j}
 (t-1)^{n-j-1}P_j(t)\quad(n\geq1).
\end{equation}
If $E_n(t)$ denotes the Eulerian polynomial normalized by
$\sum_{v\geq1}v^n t^v=tE_n(t)/(1-t)^{n+1}$, including $E_0=1$, then
\begin{equation}
 \frac{E_n(t)}{n!}=\sum_{j=0}^n\binom nj(1-t)^{n-j}\frac{P_j(t)}{j!}.
\end{equation}
The inverse replaces $E_n$ on the left by $P_n$, and $P_j$ on the right
by $E_j$ and $(1-t)^{n-j}$ by $(t-1)^{n-j}$. In particular the
alternating row sum is
\[
 P_n(-1)=n!\sum_{j=0}^n\binom nj(-2)^{n-j}\frac{E_j(-1)}{j!}.
\]

nodes.label: Corollary
nodes.next_step: Existing Lean evidence is being checked before new proof work.
nodes.statement:
Let $A_n(t)$ be the row polynomials of A131202, including $A_0=1$,
with the generating function specified in that entry \cite{related}.
Then
\begin{equation}
 A_n(t)=P_n(t)-n(t-1)P_{n-1}(t)\quad(n\geq1),\qquad
 P_n(t)=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk A_{n-k}(t)k!(t-1)^k.
\end{equation}
Consequently the multiplier sequence in its reconstruction of $P_n$
is $k!(t-1)^k$, rather than the printed
``c(n,t) = n!*(t-1)\^{}(n-1) for n > 0''.
At $n=1$ the printed rule gives $2$, whereas $P_1(t)=t$.
At $t=2$ the identity is $A_n(2)=P_n(2)-nP_{n-1}(2)$, as stated in
A084358. The binomial matrix with entries
$\binom nk A_{n-k}(2)$ is A133289 and its inverse is $2I-$A129652.
Also $A_n(1)=n!$, and $A_n(t)$ has degree $n-1$ and leading
coefficient $s_n$ for $n\geq1$, as stated in A131202.

nodes.label: Theorem
nodes.next_step: Automatic translation needs attention before a proof can be checked.
nodes.statement:
Let \(S\) be a nonempty finite semigroup and
\(\rho:S\to\operatorname{End}_k(V)\) a multiplicative map, where \(V\) is finite
dimensional over any field. Suppose every \(\rho(s)\) is singular. Put
\(d=\dim V\), \(r_s=\rank\rho(s)\), and \(t=|S|\). Then \(d\geq1\).
For every \(n\geq1\), the diagonal action on \(V^{\otimes n}\) has a finite
indecomposable decomposition, and every such decomposition, with \(b(n)\)
factors, satisfies
\begin{equation}
 d^n-2\sum_{s\in S}r_s^n\ \leq\ \mu(V^{\otimes n})\ \leq\ b(n)\ \leq\ d^n.
\end{equation}
In particular, \(b(n)/d^n\to1\), and a copy of \(Z\) is a direct summand
whenever
\begin{equation}
 n\geq1,\qquad 2\sum_{s\in S}r_s^n<d^n.
\end{equation}
Such an exponent always exists.
nodes.title: Quantitative null tensor summands for He–Tubbenhauer’s Conjecture 4.2 (arXiv:2508.04054v1, p. 17): extending their 2025 theorem

nodes.label: Corollary
nodes.next_step: Automatic translation needs attention before a proof can be checked.
nodes.statement:
Let \(M\) be a finite monoid with unit group \(G\), and let \(V\ne0\) be a
finite-dimensional unital \(kM\)-module. Suppose no element other than \(1\)
acts as the identity and \(|G|\) is invertible in \(k\). Put \(S=M\setminus G\),
\(d=\dim V\) and \(r_s=\rank\rho(s)\). For every \(n\geq1\), there is an
invariant decomposition
\[
 V^{\otimes n}=L_n\oplus U_n,\qquad S L_n=0,
 \qquad \dim U_n\leq2\sum_{s\in S}r_s^n.
\]
Consequently Conjecture~3A.2 holds under these hypotheses. If \(b_M(n)\) and
\(b_G(n)\) count indecomposable summands before and after restriction to \(G\),
then
\begin{equation}
 0\leq b_G(n)-b_M(n)\leq2\sum_{s\in S}r_s^n,
 \qquad b_M(n)/b_G(n)\longrightarrow1.
\end{equation}
When \(G=\{1\}\), over every field,
\(b_M(n)/d^n\to1\); the extra composition-ratio hypothesis of
\cite[Proposition~3C.2, p.~16]{HT25} is unnecessary.

nodes.statement:
Fix an integer $q\geq2$, a scale $t>0$ and a real $r>0$ with $r\ne1$.
There is a positive nonconstant solution of \eqref{eq:motion} on $T_q$
with the following lengths. Set
\begin{equation}
 s_n=t r^n\quad(n\in\mathbb Z),\qquad
 a=\frac{r^2+1}{r+1}.
\end{equation}
Choose a bi-infinite spine $(v_n)_{n\in\mathbb Z}$. The edge $v_nv_{n+1}$
has length $a s_n$. At each $v_n$ attach $q-1$ disjoint rooted
$q$-ary trees; every edge in these branches, including each attachment
edge, has length $s_n$. The ratio $R_i$ equals $s_n$ at $v_n$ and
at every vertex of a branch attached there.

nodes.label: Corollary
nodes.next_step: Existing Lean evidence is being checked before new proof work.
nodes.statement:
For identity return order and normalized mixed-sign rotors
$c_i^2-\varepsilon_i s_i^2=1$, put $w_i=s_i^2$ and
\[
z_i=1+\varepsilon_iw_i+\mathrm i\varepsilon_iw_i
       =\rho_i e^{\mathrm i\alpha_i},\qquad
\rho_i=\sqrt{(1+\varepsilon_iw_i)^2+w_i^2},
\]
where $\alpha_i=\operatorname{atan2}(\varepsilon_iw_i,1+\varepsilon_iw_i)$.
Then
\begin{equation}
t(\Theta_k(\mathrm{id}))
=\operatorname{Re}\!\left[(1+\mathrm i)\prod_i z_i\right]
=\sqrt2\prod_i\rho_i\,
  \cos\!\left(\frac\pi4+\sum_i\alpha_i\right).
\end{equation}
It vanishes exactly when $\sum_i\alpha_i\in\pi/4+\pi\mathbb Z$.
Zeros exist for some parameters exactly when at least two signs
$\varepsilon_i$ agree. In particular a two-factor opposite-square loop has
scalar part $1+2w_1w_2$ and never vanishes.

nodes.label: Corollary

nodes.statement:
For the square-minus-one formula, let $G_\tau$ be the graph on $I$ with
edge $\{i,j\}$ when $i<j$ and $\tau^{-1}(i)<\tau^{-1}(j)$.
Write $F_\tau(w)=t(\Theta_k(\tau))$ and let $e_\tau(S)$ count the
edges induced by $S$. Then
\begin{equation}
F_\tau(w)=\sum_{S\subseteq I}(-1)^{e_\tau(S)}
       \prod_{i\in S}w_i\prod_{i\notin S}(1-w_i).
\end{equation}
For reverse return order its range is $\{1\}$; for every other order
its range on $[0,1]^k$ is exactly $[-1,1]$, and it has a zero.
It factors across the connected components of $G_\tau$, and cannot
factor across any partition that cuts an edge. In particular it is a
product of single-variable functions exactly for reverse order.

nodes.label: Theorem
nodes.next_step: Automatic translation needs attention before a proof can be checked.
nodes.statement:
For every $n\geq1$ and $x\in\R_{\geq0}^n$,
\[
 \Dstar(x)=P(x).
\]
Every complete greedy history attains this value, independently of all
tie choices. More generally, if $x^{(0)}=x$ and
$x^{(s+1)}=T_{i_s}x^{(s)}$ describe any complete history, then
\begin{equation}
 C_H(x)-P(x)=\sum_{s=0}^{n-2}\delta_{i_s}(x^{(s)}),
 \qquad \delta_i(x)\geq0,
\end{equation}
where, writing $a=x_i$, $b=x_{i+1}$ and $m=\max(a,b)$,
\begin{align}
\delta_i(x)={}&
\begin{cases}
 \max(x_{i-1},m)-\max(x_{i-1},a),& i>1,\\
 0,&i=1
\end{cases}\notag\\
&+\begin{cases}
 \max(m,x_{i+2})-\max(b,x_{i+2}),&i+1<n,\\
 0,&i+1=n.
\end{cases}
\end{align}
Consequently, a history is optimal if and only if every one of its
merge slacks vanishes.

nodes.statement:

using the same realized readiness vector, and allow a competing policy
to use additional randomness. For every $\alpha\geq0$,
\[

 \E e^{-\alpha C_{\mathrm{greedy}}(X)}
 \geq\E e^{-\alpha C_H(X)}.

Whenever the costs are integrable, greedy histories also minimize
their expectation.

nodes.label: Corollary
nodes.next_step: Existing Lean evidence is being checked before new proof work.
nodes.statement:
Two bipartite graphs with two inputs and $n$ outputs are equivalent if
and only if they have the same $z$ and the same unordered triple
$\{a,b,c\}$, with multiplicities retained. Over all equivalent bipartite
forms, the minimum number of shared outputs is
\[
 m=\min(a,b,c)\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n-z}{3}\right\rfloor.
\]
The minimum total number of edges is $n-z+m$.
When the row rank is two, the minimum can be attained in a pivot form.
The upper bound is sharp for every $n-z\geq2$.
For two inputs, output cut ranks on singletons and pairs already determine
the row space, with the output labels fixed.

nodes.statement:
A full-rank two-input bipartite graph has no disconnected graph in its
operation-generated equivalence class exactly when $z=0$ and $a,b,c>0$.

integers summing to $n$. In particular there is exactly one such class
for $n=4$, already in \cite[Claim F, pp.~17--18]{Li} and later
\cite[Proposition 8.1, p.~22]{KL}.

nodes.statement:
For every finite-dimensional complex evolution algebra $A$,
$\Der(A)\not\cong\slie_3(\C)$ as Lie algebras. Consequently
$\AutS(A)\not\cong\mathrm{SL}_3$ as complex group schemes, and the full
automorphism algebraic group of $A$ is not $\mathrm{SL}_3$.
No condition on $A^2$ or $\Ann(A)$ is required.

nodes.statement:
Every finite direct sum $\bigoplus_a\so_{m_a}(k)$ with $m_a\ge3$ is the
derivation algebra of an evolution algebra. Thus Theorem~\ref{thm:classification}
answers exactly the semisimple clause of Question~36 in \cite[\S2.2.5, p.~25]{survey}.

nondegenerate symmetric space $(V,b)$ has an evolution algebra $E(b)$ with
$\mathbf{Aut}(E(b))\cong O(b)$ and $\Der(E(b))\cong\so(V,b)$.

nodes.label: Corollary

nodes.statement:
Suppose $\Ann(A)=0$ over an algebraically closed field of characteristic
zero. For $L=\Der(A)$, its semisimple quotient has the form
\[
 L/\rad L\cong\bigoplus_a\so_{m_a}(k),\qquad m_a\ge3.
\]
In particular, every simple ideal of $L$ is an orthogonal simple Lie
algebra. Neither $\slie_3$ nor $\mathfrak g_2$ can be such an ideal,
regardless of $\dim A^2$ or whether $L$ is semisimple.

nodes.statement:
The first three assertions of Proposition 3.2 hold throughout its stated
domain. Its singleton-sum assertion fails exactly at $(h,l)=(5,5)$.
More generally, for $r,s\ge4$, the sum assertions are
\[
 \Delta_{F_r+F_s}=F_{r-1}+F_{s-1},\qquad
 \J_{F_r+F_s}=\{v_{F_{r-1}+F_{s-1}}\},
\]
except that the degree assertion fails at $(F_r,F_s)=(3,3)$, and the
singleton assertion fails at $(3,3)$ and $(5,5)$. The pair $(3,3)$ is
outside the literal domain of Proposition 3.2 because its $t$ would be two.
At these exceptions, $\Delta_6=3$, $\J_6=\{v_3,v_4,v_5\}$ and
$\Delta_{10}=6$, $\J_{10}=\{v_6,v_7\}$. Thus both assertions hold
without exceptions if the two Fibonacci orders are distinct.

nodes.label: Corollary
nodes.next_step: Existing Lean evidence is being checked before new proof work.
nodes.statement:
The recurrence form of Conjecture 2.16.1 of \cite[p.~73]{critical}
is as follows. Set $p_0=1$ and, for $j\ge0$, define
\[
 p_{j+1}=p_j+3+2\left(\fl{(j+2)/\ph}-\fl{(j+1)/\ph}\right).
\]
The actual orders with three maximum-degree vertices are
$p_1,p_2,\ldots=6,9,14,19,22,\ldots$.
Successive increments are $3$ or $5$, with no consecutive $3$s
and no three consecutive $5$s. The order-one value is a synthetic
seed, not a graph with three maximum-degree vertices.
This is the recurrence reformulation of Patel's prior classification
\cite{patelsets}; the full maximum-set and never-singleton-label
classifications \cite{patelsets,patelnever} are separate results.
nodes.title: Refutation and correction of Theorem 2.10 (Conjectured), arXiv:1404.0484v1, Section 2, page 7: extensions of Patel (2026) and Raso–Kok (2026)

nodes.statement:
For odd $n\geq3$, a double path with its sole loop at the central
vertex allows but does not require nSSP when $n\equiv1\pmod4$,
and does not allow nSSP when $n\equiv3\pmod4$.
For every $n\geq4$, the path with loops at all interior vertices
allows but does not require nSSP; for $1\leq n\leq3$ it does not allow nSSP.
The pattern with $n=1$ and its one loop requires nSSP.
Every directed superpattern of an allowing path also allows nSSP,
with a positive-integer witness.

nodes.statement:
For fixed $n\geq0,m\geq1$, put $N=n+m$, $\lambda_S=\prod_{s\in S}s$ and
$D_S=\prod_{s\in S,t\notin S}(s-t)$. Then, as a formal power series,
\[
\sum_{k\geq0}B(n,k,m)z^k
 =\sum_{|S|=m}\frac{\lambda_S^n}{D_S(1-\lambda_S z)}.
\]
Consequently the sequence in $k$ is annihilated by
$\prod_{|S|=m}(E-\lambda_S)$, where $E$ shifts $k$ to $k+1$.

nodes.statement:
For $v\geq k\geq1$,
\[
c(v,k)=e_{v-k}(1,\ldots,v-1),\qquad
\sum_{v\geq k}c(v,k)\frac{t^v}{v!}=\frac{(-\log(1-t))^k}{k!}.
\]
For $v\geq0$ there is the polynomial identity
\[
\sum_{k=0}^v c(v,k)b^k x^{v-k}=\prod_{j=0}^{v-1}(b+jx),
\]
which includes all four families of weighted row evaluations listed by
Del\'eham (2007--2008), as well as the row sums $v!$.
For $v>k\geq1$, the two recurrences posed by Kurkov in A132393,
FORMULA (5 March 2025), are
\begin{align*}
(v-k)c(v,k)&=\sum_{j=2}^{v-k+1}\binom{-k}{j}(-1)^j c(v,k+j-1),\\
(v-k)c(v,k)&=\sum_{j=2}^{v-k+1}(j-2)!\binom vj c(v-j+1,k).
\end{align*}
The row identity already appears in the Quaintance--Gould notes (2010),
\S9.3.3, equation (9.20), there attributed to Hagen (1891)~\cite{qg}.
In that notation set $d=v-k$ and replace the summation index $j$ by $v-r$;
the binomial coefficient becomes $\binom r{k-1}$.
The column recurrence has Petrov's proof of 1 March 2025;
ploosu2 proved both by generating functions on 10 August 2025~\cite{recurrences}.
Lee gave combinatorial proofs of both in 2026~\cite[Theorems 11 and 14]{lee}.
For $v\geq1$ the weighted row sums are
\begin{gather*}
\sum_k k c(v,k)=v!H_v,\qquad
\sum_k(k\mathbin{\pm}1)c(v,k)=v!(H_v\mathbin{\pm}1),\\
\sum_k k c(v,v-k)=v!(v-H_v).
\end{gather*}
These give the first four Heinz formulas of 2 July 2026 in A132393.
In order, the sequence identifications are A000254 at $v$;
A000774 at $v$; A001705 at $v-1$; and A067318 at $v$~\cite{weighted}.

nodes.statement:
Let $A,B\in\CC^{p\times n}$, where $p,n\geq1$, and put
\[
 H=A^*B+B^*A,\qquad R=A^*A+B^*B.
\]
For every $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$,
\begin{equation}
 |\det H[S,S]|\leq\det R[S,S].
\end{equation}
Consequently, for $0\leq k\leq n$,
\begin{equation}
 \bigl|\ee_k(\lambda(H))\bigr|
 \leq\sum_{|S|=k}|\det H[S,S]|
 \leq\ee_k(\lambda(R)).
\end{equation}

nodes.statement:
With $H,R$ as in Theorem~\ref{thm:main}, for every $z\in\CC$,
\[
 |\det(\Id+zH)|\leq\det(\Id+|z|R).
\]
Moreover, $|\det H|\leq\det R$ and
$\tr R-\tr H=\|A-B\|_F^2$.
Equality in all the one-sided inequalities
$\ee_k(\lambda(H))\leq\ee_k(\lambda(R))$, $1\leq k\leq n$,
holds if and only if $A=B$.

nodes.statement:
Let $A,B,C$ be pairwise commuting positive semidefinite Hermitian matrices,
and write $S=A+B+C$, $Q=A^2+B^2+C^2$, $F=6(A^3+B^3+C^3)+S^3$.
Then $\det F\geq5^n\det S\det Q$.
For every $k$, the elementary symmetric functions of the singular values
of $F$ dominate those of $5SQ$; also
$\ee_k(\lambda(2F))\geq\ee_k(\lambda(5SQ+5QS))$.

nodes.statement:
Let $\mathbb K=\R$ or $\C$, let $1\le k$, $1\le r$, and $k+r\le n$.
Let $z_1,\ldots,z_r$ be orthonormal, set
$V=\operatorname{span}(z_1,\ldots,z_r)^\perp$, and take any
$u\in\Lambda^k V$, not necessarily decomposable. Put
$b=z_r\wedge\cdots\wedge z_1\wedge u$.
For every real array $(a_S)_{S\in\binom{[n]}k}$,
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{T\in\binom{[n]}{k+r}}\left(\min_{\substack{S\subset T\\|S|=k}}a_S\right)|b_T|^2
 \ \le\ \sum_{S\in\binom{[n]}k}a_S|u_S|^2
 \ \le\ \sum_{T\in\binom{[n]}{k+r}}\left(\max_{\substack{S\subset T\\|S|=k}}a_S\right)|b_T|^2.
\end{equation}

nodes.label: Theorem
nodes.next_step: Automatic translation needs attention before a proof can be checked.
nodes.statement:
Let $h(t)=(3t-t^3)/2$ on $[0,1]$. It is strictly increasing,
$h(1)=1$, and $h(t)/t=(3-t^2)/2$ is strictly decreasing for $0<t\le1$.
Over nonnegative unit vectors of arbitrary finite dimension,
\begin{equation}
\inf R_h(x)^2=\frac{16(17-9\sqrt3)}{23}.
\end{equation}
The infimum is not attained in a finite dimension. Restricting to at most
two nonzero coordinates gives the attained minimum $80/81$ instead.
For example, a vector with squared coordinates $(4/5,1/10,1/10)$ gives
\[
R_h(x)^2=\frac{13689}{13885}<\frac{80}{81}.
\]
The infimum in~\eqref{eq:sphereinf} is approached by one squared coordinate
$a_*=6-3\sqrt3$ and $m$ squared coordinates $(1-a_*)/m$ as $m\to\infty$.

nodes.label: Corollary

nodes.statement:
In a fragment with $n$ centres and imbalance $d$, all eigenvalues are
\begin{equation}
 E_{n,d,k}(\Delta)=\frac{\sqrt{4+9\Delta^2}}2(2k-n)
                         +\frac\Delta2d,
 \qquad\text{with multiplicity }\binom nk,\quad 0\leq k\leq n.
\end{equation}
For $\Delta\ne0$, an imbalanced fragment has a zero mode precisely
when, for an allowed $s=2k-n\ne0$,
\begin{equation}
 d^2>9s^2,\qquad
 \Delta^2=\frac{4s^2}{d^2-9s^2},\qquad s\Delta d<0.
\end{equation}
At $L=48$, centres $1,7,13,19,25,31,37,43$ and
$\Delta=2/\sqrt7$ give 56 zero modes in an imbalanced fragment.

nodes.label: Corollary
nodes.next_step: Existing Lean evidence is being checked before new proof work.
nodes.statement:
The following descriptions hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $c_e(n)$ counts primes $p$ with $p^e\le n$, and prime factors
whose exponent in $\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,n)$ is at least $e$.
For $e=2$ it also counts positive integers at most $n$ with exactly
three divisors, and is the maximum size of a pairwise coprime collection
of composite integers at most $n$.
\item For $e\ge1$, $c_e(n)=j$ exactly when
$p_j^e\le n<p_{j+1}^e$, with the $j=0$ interval $1\le n<2^e$.
As formal power series,
\[
 \sum_{n\ge1}c_e(n)x^n=\frac{\sum_{p\in\pr}x^{p^e}}{1-x}.
\]
In particular,
\[
 \sum_{n\ge1}a(n)x^n
 =\frac{\sum_{p\in\pr}x^{p^3}}{1-x}
   +x^2+x^3+x^6+x^7+x^2\sum_{j=0}^{8}x^{3j}.
\]
\item For fixed $e$, the prime number theorem gives
$c_e(n)\sim e n^{1/e}/\log n$ as $n\to\infty$. In particular,
$a(n)\sim3n^{1/3}/\log n$.
\end{enumerate}
nodes.title: Exact counts and sharp growth for OEIS A222759, first comment (12 March 2013): extending Glaisher (1900)

nodes.statement:
Let $U(N,d)=\C_d(\lfloor N/d\rfloor)$ for $1\leq d\leq N$,
the triangle A400203, revision 17, FORMULA \cite{a400203}.
Then
\begin{equation}
 U(N,d)=\sum_{\substack{q\leq N/d\\\rad(q)\mid d}}
                  M(\lfloor N/(dq)\rfloor).
\end{equation}
Its boundary and plateau formulas are
\[
 U(N,1)=M(N),\quad U(N,d)=1\ (2d>N),\quad
 U(N,d)=U(d\lfloor N/d\rfloor,d).
\]
For $1\leq d<N$, its increment is $\mob(N/d)$ when
$d\mid N$ and $(N/d,d)=1$, and zero otherwise.
Writing $H(k)=1$ if every prime exponent of $k$ is at least two,
and $H(k)=0$ otherwise, with $H(1)=1$, gives
\begin{align}
 \sum_{d=1}^{N}U(N,d)&=\sum_{k=1}^{N}H(k)
                         =\mathrm{A217038}(N+1),\\
 \sum_{d=1}^{N}\mob(d)U(N,d)&=\sum_{k=1}^{N}\mob(k)\tau(k)
                         =\mathrm{A062563}(N),\\
 \sum_{d=1}^{N}\mob(d)^2U(N,d)&=1.
\end{align}
Here $H$ is A112526, $\tau(k)$ is the number of positive divisors,
and A217038 counts powerful numbers strictly below its argument
\cite{triangle-aux}.

nodes.statement:
Write $s(d)=\sum_{k\leq d,(k,d)=1}\mob(k)^2$ (A073311 \cite{a073311}).
The formulas and data of A304575 \cite{a304575} give the sequence
\begin{equation}
 R(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}s(d)
 =\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mob\!\left(\frac{k}{(k,n)}\right)^2
 =\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mob\!\left(\frac{\operatorname{lcm}(n,k)}{n}\right)^2.
\end{equation}
Consequently $R(n)\leq n$ and
$s(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\mob(n/d)R(d)$.
If the strict inequality $k<d$ in that entry's NAME is read literally
for positive $k$, its divisor sum equals $R(n)-1$, not $R(n)$.
For $Q(t)=\sum_{1\leq k<t}\mob(k)^2$ (A013928 \cite{a013928}),
every prime $p$ and integer $m\geq0$ satisfy
\begin{align}
 R(p^{2m})&=1+\sum_{i=0}^{m}Q(p^{2i}),\\
 R(p^{2m+1})&=1+\sum_{i=0}^{m}Q(p^{2i+1}).
\end{align}

nodes.statement:
Let $d_m=\operatorname{den}(C(m,m+3))$ and $g_m=\gcd(3,m+2)$.
For every $m\ge0$,
\begin{equation}
 C(m,m+3)=\frac{(-1)^{m+1}(2m+1)}{(m+1)(m+2)},\qquad
 d_m=\frac{(m+1)(m+2)}{g_m}.
\end{equation}
Consequently, for $k\ge0$,
\begin{align}
 (d_{3k},d_{3k+1},d_{3k+2})
 &=\bigl((3k+1)(3k+2),(k+1)(3k+2),3(k+1)(3k+4)\bigr),\\

 \sum_{m\ge0}d_mz^m
 &=\frac{2(1+z+6z^2+7z^3+2z^4+3z^5+z^6)}{(1-z^3)^3}.
\end{align}
The two shifted-sequence formulas in A194767 also hold:
\[
 d_m=(m+1)\mathrm{A051176}(m+2),\qquad
 d_{m+2}=2\mathrm{A306368}(m)\quad(m\ge0).
\]
Its fourth-diagonal numerator formula requires a shift:
\begin{equation}
 C(m,m+3)=\frac{(-1)^{m+1}\mathrm{A146535}(m+1)}{d_m},
 \quad\text{not }\frac{(-1)^{m+1}\mathrm{A146535}(m)}{d_m}.
\end{equation}

nodes.statement:
Let $P_0(x)=1$, $P_1(x)=3+x$ and
$P_m=(x+2)P_{m-1}-P_{m-2}$ for $m\geq2$. Then
\[
[x^k]P_m=b_{m+k+1,k}
=\binom{m+k}{2k}+2\binom{m+k}{2k+1}\quad(0\leq k\leq m).
\]
These are Andr\'e-Jeannin's $r=2$ coefficient theorem (1994,
equation~(9)) and the array A111125 \cite{andre,related-arrays}.

nodes.statement:
With $P_m$ as above and $z$ invertible,
\[
z^{2m+1}-z^{-(2m+1)}=(z-z^{-1})P_m((z-z^{-1})^2).
\]
Consequently, with the usual Fibonacci numbers $F_n$ and Lucas numbers $L_n$,
\[
P_m(1)=L_{2m+1},\qquad
F_{(2m+1)n}=\sum_{k=0}^m[x^k]P_m(x)\,
(-1)^{(m+k)n}5^kF_n^{2k+1}\quad(n\geq0).
\]
The values $P_m(-1)$ repeat $1,2,1,-1,-2,-1$. For $m\geq1$,
\[
P_m(x)=\prod_{j=1}^m\left(x+4\sin^2\frac{j\pi}{2m+1}\right).
\]
These are established Morgan--Voyce and A111125 identities
\cite{andre,related-arrays}.

nodes.statement:
For $d\geq2$ and $m\geq0$,
\begin{align}
h_d(m)&=\binom{m+d-1}{d-1}+\binom{m+d-2}{d-1}\\
&=2\binom{m+d-1}{d-1}-\binom{m+d-2}{d-2}
=\frac{2m+d-1}{d-1}\binom{m+d-2}{d-2}.\nonumber
\end{align}
Moreover $h_{d+1}(m)=\sum_{j=0}^m h_d(j)$ and
\[
h_d(m)=\sum_{j=1}^d(-1)^{j+1}\binom dj h_d(m-j)\qquad(m\geq d).
\]
As a polynomial in $m$, $h_d$ has degree $d-1$, leading coefficient
$2/(d-1)!$, and symmetry $h_d(-m-d+1)=(-1)^{d-1}h_d(m)$.

nodes.statement:
For $n\geq1$ and $d\geq2$,
\[
\sum_{j=0}^n(-1)^j h_d(j)
\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-j+1)}{(n+d)(n+d+1)\cdots(n+d+j-1)}=0,
\]
where an empty product is $1$. This is Bala's terminating identity (2019)
in A005585, A040977, A050486 and A053347 \cite{columns}.
If $p>d-1$ is prime and $e\geq1$, then $p^e\mid h_d(m)$ whenever
$m+j\equiv0\pmod{p^e}$ for some $1\leq j\leq d-2$, or
$2m+d-1\equiv0\pmod{p^e}$.

nodes.statement:
Let $d\geq4$ and $m\geq0$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item In a set $X$ of size $m+d$, take disjoint subsets $Y,Z$ of sizes
$2$ and $m+d-3$. The number of $d$-subsets meeting both is $h_d(m)$.
\item The number of placements of $d-2$ queens on an
$(m+d-2)\times(m+d-2)$ board in distinct rows and columns, with every pair
attacking diagonally, is $2h_d(m)$.
\item For the Chebyshev polynomials $T_0(t)=1$, $T_1(t)=t$,
$T_{j+1}(t)=2tT_j(t)-T_{j-1}(t)$, and $r=d-1$,
\[
[t^r]T_{r+2m}(t)=(-1)^m2^{r-1}h_d(m).
\]
\item The order polytope of a chain of $d-3$ elements below two
incomparable elements has $h_d(m)$ lattice points in its $m$th dilation.
\end{enumerate}

Then
\[
a_m+ib_m=(1+2i)(1-i)^m,\qquad a_{m+4}=-4a_m,\quad b_{m+4}=-4b_m.

$b_0,\ldots,b_3=2,1,-2,-6$ and $b_{18}=-512$.
If $\alpha=\arctan 2$, the continuous polar angle is

\[
a_m=A B^{\theta_m}\cos\theta_m,\qquad
b_m=A B^{\theta_m}\sin\theta_m,
\quad A=\sqrt5\,16^{\alpha/(2\pi)},\ B=16^{-1/(2\pi)}.

nodes.statement:
The difference sequence is a concatenation of
$(1,1,1,-3)$ and $(1,1,1,1,-3)$. The first block has length five.
For $j\geq1$, let
\begin{equation}
 R_j=\floor{\frac{j^2+5j+7}{8}}.
\end{equation}
Apart from the first block, the blocks of length five have precisely
the block indices $r=R_j$, where the block indexed by $r$ starts at
difference index $n_r$. Their starting indices are $4R_j+j$.
Between the length-five blocks indexed by $R_j$ and $R_{j+1}$ there are
exactly $R_{j+1}-R_j-1=j/4+O(1)$ length-four blocks.
Furthermore,
\begin{equation}
 \alpha_n\leq a(n)<\alpha_n+4,\qquad
 a(n)=\sqrt{2n}+O(1),\qquad
 \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{a(n)}{\sqrt{2n}}=1.
\end{equation}

nodes.statement:
For every $n\geq0$,
\[
 t(n)=\floor{\frac{2n+5-\sqrt{8n+17}}4},\qquad b(n)=n-2t(n),
 \qquad b(n)=\sqrt{2n}+O(1).
\]
The absolute-mode difference sequence consists of $(1,-1)$ and $(1,1,-1)$.
Its initial block has length three. Apart from that initial block, its
length-three blocks have indices
\[
 L_j=\floor{\frac{(j+1)(j+2)}4},\qquad j\geq1,
\]
and start at difference indices $2L_j+j$.
At every degree with two absolute maxima the two maximizing exponents
are $b(n)$ and $b(n)+2$, their coefficients have opposite signs,
and $B(n)=M(n)$.
More generally, $B(n)=M(n)$ if and only if either there are two absolute
maxima or $t(n)$ is even.
The signed and absolute modes interlace in the precise sense
$a(n)\in\{b(n)-2,b(n),b(n)+2\}$ for every $n\geq0$.

nodes.statement:
Assume~\eqref{fitting} and $\mu\ge3$. Define
\[
 t=b_1-a_\mu,\qquad
 c=\begin{cases}\mu,&a_1>0,\\ \mu-1,&a_1=0,\end{cases}
 \qquad d=\sum_{i=1}^{\mu}a_i(b_i-a_i).
\]
Then $\deg P=d$, $d\ge t+4$, and
\begin{equation}
 \coeff{j}{P}=0\ (j<t+1),\quad
 \coeff{t+1}{P}=1,\quad \coeff{t+2}{P}=c+1,\quad
 \coeff{d-1}{P}=c,\quad \coeff{d}{P}=1.
\end{equation}
In particular, $P$ is not almost palindromic, proving Conjecture 9.63.
The same conclusions hold at width two if
$a_2-a_1\ge2$ and $b_2-b_1\ge2$.

nodes.label: Corollary
nodes.next_step: Automatic translation needs attention before a proof can be checked.
nodes.statement:
Let $M(\lambda)$ and $N(\lambda)$ be the sets in Okada's Conjecture 9.64:
$M(\lambda)$ consists of all $0\le a_1<a_2\le b_1<b_2=\lambda$, and
$N(\lambda)$ consists of those tuples whose determinant is not almost
palindromic. For $\lambda\ge2$,
\[
 |M(\lambda)|=\binom{\lambda+1}{3},\quad
 |N(\lambda)|=\binom{\lambda-1}{3},\quad
 |M(\lambda)\setminus N(\lambda)|=(\lambda-1)^2,
\]
where a binomial coefficient with upper index less than three is zero.
Consequently
\begin{equation}
 O(\lambda)=\frac{|N(\lambda)|}{|M(\lambda)|}
           =\frac{(\lambda-2)(\lambda-3)}{\lambda(\lambda+1)}.
\end{equation}
In particular, $O(3)=0$, $O(\lambda+1)>O(\lambda)$ for $\lambda\ge3$,
and $O(\lambda)\longrightarrow1$.
nodes.title: Proofs of Okada's Conjectures 9.63 and 9.64 with constant-base-shift extensions (arXiv:2003.02112v2, Section 9.8.3)

nodes.statement:
Assume~\eqref{fitting} with $\mu\ge2$. For any $\rho\ge1$, put
$G=\deg A_\rho-\deg B_\rho$.
Then
\[
 q^{d_\rho}P_{\rho,G}(q^{-1})=P_{\rho,0}(q).

permutation matrices:
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
A&xy\mid uv&xv\mid yu\\
B&uz\mid pw&uw\mid zp\\
C&vw\mid qr&vr\mid wq.
\end{array}
\]
For ordinary unitary quantum gates, the same equivalence holds with
``unitary'' in place of ``permutation''.

nodes.statement:
Let $p$ be an odd prime, $V=\F_p^n$, and $d=p^n$. Suppose $\Sset$ consists of $d$ symmetric $n\times n$ matrices over $\F_p$, contains zero, and every difference of distinct matrices is invertible. For $M\in\Sset$ and $b\in V$, set
\[
f_{M,b}(x)=x^TMx+b^Tx,\quad
\phi_{M,b}(x)=\frac{2\pi}{p}f_{M,b}(x)\pmod {2\pi},\quad
X(\Sset)=\{\phi_{M,b}:M\in\Sset,\ b\in V\}.
\]
Then $X(\Sset)$ has $d^2$ points, contains zero, is anchored at $x=0$, satisfies \eqref{eq:moment} and \eqref{eq:overlap}, and is a subgroup if and only if $\Sset$ is closed under matrix addition.

nodes.label: Theorem

nodes.statement:
Fix $r\geq3$ and distinct odd primes $q_1,\ldots,q_{r-3}$, with an empty
list when $r=3$. For every integer $K\geq2$, put
\[
 u_{r,K}(n)=1+2^n+2^{Kn}+\sum_{i=1}^{r-3}q_i^n.
\]
This is a positive integer sequence of rank $r$, and its general rank
sequence is
\begin{equation}
 H_{r,K}(M)=\binom{M+r-1}{r-1}-
 \begin{cases}\binom{M-K+r-1}{r-1},&M\geq K,\\0,&M<K.\end{cases}
\end{equation}
Different $K$ give different rank sequences. For $M\geq K$ the displayed
expression is a polynomial of degree $r-2$ with leading coefficient
$K/(r-2)!$.
nodes.title: Infinitely many general rank sequences: extending Patel's polynomiality picture (2026) at arXiv:2501.14643v1, Section 1, p. 2

nodes.statement:
The row sums $U_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}D^+_{n,k}$ and
$L_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}D^-_{n,k}$ are
\begin{align*}
U_n&=\frac{n^2(n+1)(2n+1)+3n(n+\eps)}{12},\\
L_n&=\frac{n^2(n^2+1)}2+T_n-U_n.
\end{align*}
These are the defining formulas of A325517 and A325656
(Spezia, 2019)~\cite{s325517,s325656}. Also
$D^+_{n,n-1}=n$, while $D^-_{n,n-1}$ equals $n^2$ for even $n$
and $n^2-n+1$ for odd $n$, as in A325657~\cite{s325657}.
Writing $Q(z)=(1-z)^5(1+z)^2$, one has
\begin{align*}
\sum_{n\geq0}U_nz^n&=\frac{z(1+3z+7z^2+3z^3+2z^4)}{Q(z)},\\
\sum_{n\geq0}L_nz^n&=\frac{z(1+5z+13z^2+9z^3+4z^4)}{Q(z)},\\
\sum_{n\geq0}L_n\frac{z^n}{n!}
&=\frac{z}{24}\left(3e^{-z}+(21+78z+54z^2+8z^3)e^z\right).
\end{align*}

nodes.statement:
Put $h_n=n^2(n^2-1)/12$ and $g_n=n^2(n^2+1)/2$. For $n\geq2$, let
$N^+_{ij}=i+j$ and $N^-_{ij}=i-j$, with $1\leq i,j\leq n$. Then
\[
\det(xI-N^+)=x^{n-2}(x^2-n(n+1)x-h_n),\qquad
\det(xI-N^-)=x^{n-2}(x^2+h_n).
\]
Both matrices have rank two, and
$h_n=\tfrac12\sum_{i,j=1}^n(i-j)^2$ (Bala, 2007, A002415).
The ordinary and exponential generating functions of $h_n$ are
\[
\sum_{n\geq0}h_nz^n=\frac{z^2(1+z)}{(1-z)^5},\qquad
\sum_{n\geq0}h_n\frac{z^n}{n!}
=\frac{e^zz^2(6+6z+z^2)}{12}.
\]
The reciprocal formulas recorded in A002415 and A037270 are
\begin{align*}
\sum_{n\geq2}\frac1{h_n}&=21-2\pi^2,&
\sum_{n\geq2}\frac{(-1)^n}{h_n}&=\pi^2-9,\\
\sum_{n\geq1}\frac1{g_n}&=1+\frac{\pi^2}{3}-\pi\coth\pi,&
\sum_{n\geq1}\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{g_n}
&=\pi\operatorname{csch}\pi+\frac{\pi^2}{6}-1.
\end{align*}
The nonalternating identities are attributed to Kotesovec (2016 for $h_n$,
2019 for $g_n$), and the alternating ones to Eldar (2020 for $h_n$,
2021 for $g_n$), in those records.

nodes.statement:
For every set $U$ and every nonzero commutative unitary ring $R$,
$S_U$ is a commutative periodic monoid and
\begin{equation}

nodes.label: Proposition
nodes.next_step: Automatic translation needs attention before a proof can be checked.
nodes.statement:
The negative-sum counts, namely A344608, satisfy
$N(m)\le N(m+1)$ for every $m\ge0$, answering its COMMENTS
monotonicity question \cite{a344608}.
The COMMENTS of A344743 say exactly ``Conjecture: a(n) >= A236914.''
\cite{a344743}, without specifying the argument on the right.
A common-index reading is not asserted explicitly in the source;
it fails at $n=1$, with sides $0$ and $1$.
A precise valid comparison is
\begin{equation}
 \mathrm{A344743}(n+1)\ \ge\ \mathrm{A236914}(n)
 \qquad(n\ge0).
\end{equation}
Equality in \eqref{eq:corrected} holds exactly for $n=0,1,2,3$;
for $n\ge4$ its deficit is at least $\lfloor(n-4)/2\rfloor+1$.
More generally, $N(m)=N(m+1)$ exactly for
$m\in\{0,1,3,5,7\}$.
By conjugation, $N(m)$ also counts partitions with even largest part
and at least one odd part. In particular, the odd-weight identity is
$N(2n+1)=E(2n+1)$; the index $2n+2$ and the phrase concerning parts
not all odd in the COMMENTS of A344608 require these corrections.

nodes.label: Proposition

nodes.statement:
Let $d(0)=1$, and for $r\ge1$ let $d(r)$ count distinct-part partitions
of $2r$ with odd length, namely A344650$(r)$.
Then
\begin{equation}
 C(2n)=\sum_{r=0}^n d(r)p(n-r).
\end{equation}
Conjugation also identifies the partitions counted by $C(m)$ with
partitions of $m$ whose largest part is odd or whose parts are all even,
with the empty partition included in the latter class.
More generally, let $B_m(s)$ and $D_m(s)$ count unrestricted and
distinct-part partitions of $m$ with $R=s$. Then for every integer $s$,
\begin{equation}
 B_m(s)=\sum_{t=0}^{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}p(t)D_{m-2t}(s).
\end{equation}

nodes.statement:
For every $n,d\geq3$, define
\[
 T=d^2-3d+3,\quad

 p_* =\frac{(d-2)^2}{Tk},\quad

\]
with $k$ as in \eqref{eq:rank}. Then $0<p_*<1$, $w(p_*)=w_*$, and

                  \leq \EG(\rho(p_*)).

In particular, for $n=d=3$ one has $p_*=3/8$ and
\begin{equation}

       <\frac{13}{108}\leq\EG(\rho_{3,3}(3/8)).
